title: The final Amen (CCC 2855–2865)
hookLine: the Catechism ends where prayer ends: Amen

cards: A thick book on a table. It holds the creed line by line, the sacraments one by one, the commandments, and then a long walk through prayer. Turn to its very last paragraph, and what it's talking about is one small word.
Not a doctrine. Not a rule. A word said at the end of prayers, often without a thought.
The Catechism of the Catholic Church closes on Amen. We've read it part by part since the start of this year, and today we reach that same last word. Today: the final Amen.

teach.b: First, what comes just before it. In the Douay-Rheims, Matthew's Our Father ends simply: "But deliver us from evil. Amen."

Christians who use the King James wording go on: "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever." At Mass, Catholics say words of praise much like these, after a short prayer by the priest.
The Catechism says this praise gathers up the first three petitions, the name, the kingdom, the will, and hands them back to God. Then the Amen, which you met at Mass back on day one hundred fifteen.

teach.h: AMEN: SO BE IT, A SEAL.
teach.b: The Catechism quotes Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching new Christians: after the prayer, you say Amen, which means so be it, and so put your seal on everything the prayer contains. A signature at the bottom of a letter.

In its final paragraph the Catechism goes one step further: the last Amen is our own yes to all seven petitions. Days ago we met Mary's yes at the angel's word. Here everyone who prays gets to say one like it.

And in Revelation, Christ himself is given the name: "These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness." So for Catholics the word that ends the prayer is also a name for the one it goes through. Now look back.
The Catechism has four parts, and we've walked them all this year: what the Church believes, how it celebrates, how it lives, how it prays. It ends with a word a small child can say.

how: Catholics end their prayers with Amen and answer Amen many times during Mass, including when receiving Communion; at Mass, the Our Father is followed by a short prayer of the priest and then the people's words of praise to God's kingdom, power and glory.

o: a Latin word meaning peace be with you
a polite way to tell God the prayer is over
so be it: a seal of yes on everything prayed

p: a name for Christ in Revelation

s: the Douay-Rheims Our Father in Matthew includes for thine is the kingdom
it ends "But deliver us from evil. Amen." the King James wording adds the words of praise.
Cyril of Jerusalem taught that saying Amen seals what the prayer contains
the Catechism quotes him: Amen means so be it.
the Catechism ends with a long list of rules
its last paragraph is about the final Amen: our yes to every petition.

games.q: you're a new Christian, hearing Cyril of Jerusalem explain the Our Father. you reach the last word. what does he tell you it does?
o: it simply means the prayer is over.
it means so be it, sealing what was prayed.
it's a word only the priest may say.
games.why: Cyril, quoted in the Catechism: after the prayer you say Amen, which means so be it, and so you seal what God has taught you to ask.

practice: If you pray, choose one line of the Our Father you most want to mean today, say it, and answer it with one deliberate Amen, like a signature; take another line if there's time.
If you don't pray, think back over these months, one belief, one sacrament, one way of living, one prayer that stayed with you, and let them rest together.

wordCard.voice: The final Amen. The last word of the Our Father, and the subject of the Catechism's last paragraph: so be it, our yes to everything the prayer asks.

orig.note: Hebrew: amen — a word from the Hebrew scriptures; Cyril explains it as "so be it."

carryVoice: Your line: amen. Tomorrow a new part begins, with a boy locked in a tower. Go gently.
